No verb 'to be'. Both halves are marfūʿ.en: Arabic just puts the two words side by side: ‘I engineer’. There’s no word for ‘is’ in the present.

The demonstrative agrees in gender with.h: ‘This’ has a male and a female form
The demonstrative agrees in gender with.tr: This is a student (m) · This is a student (f).
The demonstrative agrees in gender with.en: Use هَذا for a man or a masculine word, and هَذِهِ for a woman or a feminine word (most end in ة).

Add ـِيّ to a country to make a national.h: Turning a country into a nationality
Add ـِيّ to a country to make a national.en: Add ـِيّ to the country to say where someone is from. For a woman, add ة as well: ـِيَّة.

ما asks about things, مَنْ about people,.tr: What? · Who? · Is…? / Are…? · Where from?
ما asks about things, مَنْ about people,.en: ما asks ‘what’, مَنْ asks ‘who’, and مِنْ أَيْنَ asks ‘where from’. Put هَلْ at the start of a sentence to make it a yes/no question.

Two nouns joined: the first takes no ال.h: ‘The X of Y’: two nouns side by side
Two nouns joined: the first takes no ال.en: Say the thing first, then whose it is: ‘picture family-my’. The first word never takes ال or the extra -n; the second ends in -i (here hidden under ـِي, ‘my’).

Possession is a suffix on the noun, not.tr: my father · your father · his father
Possession is a suffix on the noun, not.en: Instead of a separate word, Arabic adds an ending: ـِي for ‘my’, ـكَ for ‘your’, ـهُ for ‘his’.

The prefix carries the person: أ for 'I'.h: Who’s doing it? Look at the first letter
The prefix carries the person: أ for 'I'.tr: I make wudu · he makes wudu
The prefix carries the person: أ for 'I'.en: In the present tense, the first letter shows who: أ for ‘I’, يـ for ‘he’, تـ for ‘she’ or ‘you’.

The counted noun comes after, in the plu.en: The number comes first, then the thing you’re counting, in the plural and ending in -in.

'There is' sentences put the place first.tr: There is a bed in the room.
'There is' sentences put the place first.en: Start with the place, then the thing: ‘in the room, a bed’. There’s no separate word for ‘there is’.

With a feminine noun the number drops it.en: With a feminine word (most end in ة, like غُرْفَة), say the number without ة: خَمْسُ غُرَفٍ. With a masculine word, add ة: خَمْسَةُ أَوْلادٍ. It feels backwards, but that’s the rule.

After كَمْ the noun is singular and manṣ.en: After كَمْ, use the singular word ending in -an: ‘how many room?’. Never the plural.

Ordinals follow the noun and match it in.en: Arabic says ‘the floor the fifth’: the number word comes after the noun and copies it, so if the noun has ال, so does the number.

The present tense covers habits: 'I wake.en: The same verb means ‘I wake up’, ‘I’m waking up’ and ‘I usually wake up’. The situation tells you which.

These adverbs are manṣūb — they always e.en: Words that say how or when you do something usually end in -an (ـًا).

بِـ marks the means of transport, and ta.en: Put بِـ on the front of the transport. The word after it ends in -i.

لا negates the present tense; ما is for.en: Put لا before a present-tense verb. (For the past you’ll use ما later on.)

The object of a verb is manṣūb — fatḥa,.h: ‘I eat rice’: verb, then the thing
The object of a verb is manṣūb — fatḥa,.en: Say the verb, then the thing: ‘I eat the rice’. Small detail: the thing gets an -a sound at the end, as in الأَرُزَّ.

Accusative before عَلى, genitive after i.en: أُفَضِّلُ + what you like more + عَلى + the other thing. The first ends in -a, the one after عَلى in -i.

لِأَنَّ needs a noun after it, and that.en: لِأَنَّ means ‘because’. It’s followed by a noun, or by an ending like ـها (‘it’), rather than straight by a verb.

The فَعْلان pattern is a diptote — no ta.en: Words like جَوْعان (hungry) and عَطْشان (thirsty) never add the extra -n sound: جَوْعانُ, not جَوْعانٌ.

'Going' is an adjective here, not a verb.tr: going (said by a man) · going (said by a woman)
'Going' is an adjective here, not a verb.en: أَنا ذاهِبٌ is literally ‘I (am) going’. It works like a describing word, so a woman adds ة: أَنا ذاهِبَةٌ.

لِـ means 'for the purpose of', and take.en: لِـ on the front of a word means ‘for’. The word after it ends in -i.

Place names like مَكَّة take a fatḥa whe.en: Some names, like مَكَّة, keep a simple ending: you say إِلى مَكَّةَ (to Makkah), never مَكَّةٍ.

Compound prepositions end in a genitive.en: These place words go straight before the noun, and the noun ends in -i.

After لِـ the verb takes a fatḥa — the s.en: Put لِـ on a present-tense verb to say ‘in order to’. The verb then ends in -a: أَدْرُسَ, not أَدْرُسُ.

Singular and manṣūb after كَمْ, however.en: The same rule as before: after كَمْ, use the singular word ending in -an.

'College of Education' — the second noun.en: Two nouns side by side mean ‘X of Y’. Only the second one takes ال, and it ends in -i.

Plural masculine verbs end in ـُونَ in t.en: For ‘they’ meaning men or a mixed group, the present verb starts with يَـ and ends in ـُونَ.

Doubling the middle letter turns 'do' in.h: Doubling a letter changes the meaning
Doubling the middle letter turns 'do' in.en: The shadda (ّ) doubles the middle letter and often means ‘make someone do it’: study → teach.

Nouns ending in ى never change their end.h: Words ending in ى don’t change
Nouns ending in ى never change their end.en: Words ending in ى, like مُسْتَشْفى (hospital), keep the same ending whatever comes before them.

Most job names form the feminine by addi.en: Most job words become feminine by adding ة, just like nationalities.

Same rule as always after كَمْ: singular.tr: How many hours do you work?
Same rule as always after كَمْ: singular.en: The same كَمْ rule: one hour, ending in -an: ساعَةً.

Prices use بِكَمْ, not كَمْ on its own..en: For prices, say بِكَمْ (‘for how much?’). كَمْ on its own asks ‘how many?’.

The thing wanted is the object, so it an.en: The thing you want takes the -a ending, and so does its colour: قَمِيصًا أَبْيَضَ.

The أَفْعَل colour pattern never takes t.en: Colours like أَبْيَض and أَزْرَق never end in -un or -an. Where other words take -an, they just take -a.

After 11–99 the counted noun is singular.en: After numbers from 11 to 99, the thing you’re counting is singular and ends in -an: ‘fifty riyal’.

كانَ leaves the subject marfūʿ but makes.en: Use كانَ for ‘was’. It makes the describing word end in -an: بارِدًا.

لَيْسَ behaves exactly like كانَ — predi.en: لَيْسَ means ‘is not’. Like كانَ, it makes the describing word end in -an.

لِذَلِكَ introduces a result; لِأَنَّ in.tr: It’s raining, so I took the umbrella.
لِذَلِكَ introduces a result; لِأَنَّ in.en: لِذَلِكَ means ‘so’ (what happened as a result). لِأَنَّ means ‘because’ (the reason). Don’t mix them up.

An iḍāfa: 'the season of spring'..en: Arabic says ‘season (of) the spring’: two nouns side by side, the second with ال and ending in -i.

لَكِنَّ with shadda takes a noun and mak.en: لَكِنَّ (with a shadda) is followed by a noun ending in -a. لَكِنْ (without one) can go before anything and changes nothing.

To say 'there isn't', use لَيْسَ, not لا.tr: There isn’t any crowding in the village.
To say 'there isn't', use لَيْسَ, not لا.en: Start with لَيْسَ, then the place, then the thing. Don’t use لا for this.

The فَعْلاء pattern is a diptote — never.en: For a feminine word the colour changes: أَبْيَض → بَيْضاء, أَزْرَق → زَرْقاء. These never add the extra -n either.

Duals end in ـانِ when marfūʿ and ـَيْنِ.en: Add ـانِ to mean ‘two’: ساعَة → ساعَتانِ, ‘two hours’. In some sentences it becomes ـَيْنِ instead, as here. You’ll hear both.

Both halves marfūʿ; no verb needed..en: As in unit 1, just put the two parts side by side. Both keep their usual -u ending.

Sound feminine plurals take a kasra in t.en: Many feminine words make their plural with ـات: مَجَلَّة → مَجَلَّات (magazines). Small detail: these never end in -an; you’ll hear -in instead.

When the reason refers back to something.en: Join ‘it’, ‘he’ or ‘I’ straight onto لِأَنَّ: لِأَنَّها ‘because it (f)’, لِأَنَّهُ ‘because he / it’, لِأَنَّنِي ‘because I’.

A defective verb — the final ى doesn't c.en: Some verbs end in ى, like أَهْوى (‘I love doing’). The ى stays the same.

drills.I eat ___ . All four take the accusative: I eat ___ . All four are what you eat, so they end in -a (or -an).
drills.I prefer ___ to ___ . Accusative on the: I prefer ___ to ___ . The word before عَلَى ends in -a, the word after it in -i: that’s the whole drill.
drills.I'm going to ___ . Note مَكَّةَ takes no: I'm going to ___ . Note مَكَّةَ ends in -a, not -i: names like this never take -i.
drills.I go to ___ to study ___ . Note أَدْرُسَ: I go to ___ to study ___ . Note أَدْرُسَ ends in -a after لِـ (‘in order to’).
